{{Short description|Probability and computer science concept}}
In [[probability theory]] and [[theoretical computer science]], '''McDiarmid's inequality''' (named after Colin McDiarmid <ref>{{cite journal |last1=McDiarmid |first1=Colin |title=On the method of bounded differences |journal=Surveys in Combinatorics, 1989: Invited Papers at the Twelfth British Combinatorial Conference |date=1989 |pages=148–188|doi=10.1017/CBO9781107359949.008 |isbn=978-0-521-37823-9 }}</ref>) is a [[concentration inequality]] which bounds the deviation between the sampled value and the [[expected value]] of certain functions when they are evaluated on [[independent random variables]]. McDiarmid's inequality applies to functions that satisfy a ''bounded differences'' property, meaning that replacing a single argument to the function while leaving all other arguments unchanged cannot cause too large of a change in the value of the function.

==Statement==
A function <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> satisfies the ''bounded differences property'' if substituting the value of the <math>i</math>th coordinate <math>x_i</math> changes the value of <math>f</math> by at most <math>c_i</math>. More formally, if there are constants <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math> such that for all <math>i\in[n]</math>, and all <math>x_1\in \mathcal{X}_1,\,x_2\in \mathcal{X}_2,\, \ldots,\, x_n \in \mathcal{X}_n</math>,
:<math>
\sup_{x_i' \in \mathcal{X}_i} \left|f(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}, x_i, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}, x_i', x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n)\right| \leq c_i.
</math>

{{math theorem|name=McDiarmid's Inequality<ref name=Doob>
{{cite journal |last=Doob |first=J. L. |year=1940 |title=Regularity properties of certain families of chance variables |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=455–486 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1940-047-03/S0002-9947-1940-0002052-6/S0002-9947-1940-0002052-6.pdf |doi=10.2307/1989964|jstor=1989964 |doi-access=free }}
</ref>|math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n  \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> satisfy the bounded differences property with bounds <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math>.

Consider independent random variables <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.
Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}\left(f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)] \geq \varepsilon\right)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2} \right),
</math>
:<math>
\text{P}(f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)] \leq -\varepsilon)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2}\right),
</math>
and as an immediate consequence,
:<math>
\text{P}(|f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)]| \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
2 \exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2}\right).
</math>
}}

==Extensions==

===Unbalanced distributions===

A stronger bound may be given when the arguments to the function are sampled from unbalanced distributions, such that resampling a single argument rarely causes a large change to the function value.

{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (unbalanced)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chou |first1=Chi-Ning |last2=Love |first2=Peter J. |last3=Sandhu |first3=Juspreet Singh |last4=Shi |first4=Jonathan |title=Limitations of Local Quantum Algorithms on Random MAX-k-XOR and Beyond |journal=49th International Colloquium on Automata, Languages, and Programming (ICALP 2022) |date=2022 |volume=229 |page=41:13 |publisher=Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2022.41 |doi-access=free |url=https://drops.dagstuhl.de/opus/volltexte/2022/16382/ |arxiv=2108.06049 |access-date=8 July 2022}}</ref><ref name="ying">{{cite web |last1=Ying |first1=Yiming |title=McDiarmid's inequalities of Bernstein and Bennett forms |date=2004 |website=City University of Hong Kong |url=http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/Y.Ying/McDiarmid.pdf |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref>|math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> satisfy the bounded differences property with bounds <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math>.

Consider independent random variables <math>X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{X}</math> drawn from a distribution where there is a particular value <math>\chi_0 \in \mathcal{X}</math> which occurs with probability <math>1-p</math>.
Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}(|f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)]| \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
2 \exp \left(\frac{-\varepsilon^2}{2p(2-p)\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2 + \frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\max_i c_i}\right).
</math>
}}

This may be used to characterize, for example, the value of a function on [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] when evaluated on sparse [[random graphs]] and [[hypergraphs]], since in a sparse random graph, it is much more likely for any particular edge to be missing than to be present.

===Differences bounded with high probability===

McDiarmid's inequality may be extended to the case where the function being analyzed does not strictly satisfy the bounded differences property, but large differences remain very rare.

{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (Differences bounded with high probability)<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last1=Combes |first1=Richard |title=An extension of McDiarmid's inequality |year=2015 |class=cs.LG |eprint=1511.05240 }}</ref> |math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n  \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> be a function and <math>\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n</math> be a subset of its domain and let <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n \ge 0</math> be constants such that for all pairs <math>(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in \mathcal{Y}</math> and <math>(x'_1,\ldots,x'_n)\in \mathcal{Y}</math>,
:<math>
\left|f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) - f(x'_1, \ldots, x'_n)\right| \leq \sum_{i: x_i \ne x'_i} c_i.
</math>

Consider independent random variables <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.
Let <math>p = 1 - \mathrm{P}((X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{Y})</math> and let <math>m=\mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \mid (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{Y}]</math>.
Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}\left(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - m \geq \varepsilon\right)
\leq p +
\exp \left(-\frac{2 \max\left(0,\varepsilon-p\sum_{i=1}^nc_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2} \right),
</math>
and as an immediate consequence,
:<math>
\text{P}(|f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - m| \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
2p+2\exp \left(-\frac{2 \max\left(0,\varepsilon-p\sum_{i=1}^nc_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2} \right).
</math>
}}

There exist stronger refinements to this analysis in some distribution-dependent scenarios,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Xinxing |last2=Zhang |first2=Junping |title=Distribution-dependent concentration inequalities for tighter generalization bounds |journal=Science China Information Sciences |date=April 2018 |volume=61 |issue=4 |pages=048105:1–048105:3 |doi=10.1007/s11432-017-9225-2 |arxiv=1607.05506 |s2cid=255199895 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11432-017-9225-2 |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> such as those that arise in [[Statistical learning theory|learning theory]].
<!--Note: I think the following reference is strictly generalized by Combes's result. <ref>{{cite web |last1=Kutin |first1=Samuel |title=Extensions to McDiarmid’s inequality when differences are bounded with high probability |url=https://newtraell.cs.uchicago.edu/files/tr_additional/TR-2002-04.pdf |website=University of Chicago Department of Computer Science |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref>-->

===Sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential norms===

Let the ''<math>k</math>th centered conditional version'' of a function <math>f</math> be
: <math>f_k(X)(x) := f(x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, X_k, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n) - \mathbb{E}_{X'_k}f(x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, X'_k, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n),</math>
so that <math>f_k(X)</math> is a random variable depending on random values of <math>x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1}, x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n</math>.

{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (Sub-Gaussian norm)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kontorovich |first1=Aryeh |title=Concentration in unbounded metric spaces and algorithmic stability |journal=Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Machine Learning |date=22 June 2014 |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=28–36 |arxiv=1309.1007 |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v32/kontorovicha14.html |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref><ref name="subexponential">{{cite journal |last1=Maurer |first1=Andreas |last2=Pontil |first2=Pontil |title=Concentration inequalities under sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential conditions |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |date=2021 |volume=34 |pages=7588–7597 |url=https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/3e33b970f21d2fc65096871ea0d2c6e4-Paper.pdf |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> |math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n  \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> be a function.
Consider independent random variables <math>X = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.

Let <math>f_k(X)</math> refer to the <math>k</math>th centered conditional version of <math>f</math>.
Let <math>\|\cdot\|_{\psi_2}</math> denote the [[sub-Gaussian norm]] of a random variable.

Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}\left(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - m \geq \varepsilon\right)
\leq
\exp \left(\frac{-\varepsilon^2}{32e\left\|\sum_{k\in [n]}\|f_k(X)\|_{\psi_2}^2\right\|_{\infty}} \right).
</math>
}}

{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (Sub-exponential norm)<ref name="subexponential" /> |math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n  \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> be a function.
Consider independent random variables <math>X = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.

Let <math>f_k(X)</math> refer to the <math>k</math>th centered conditional version of <math>f</math>.
Let <math>\|\cdot\|_{\psi_1}</math> denote the [[sub-exponential norm]] of a random variable.

Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}\left(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - m \geq \varepsilon\right)
\leq
\exp \left(\frac{-\varepsilon^2}{4e^2\left\|\sum_{k\in [n]}\|f_k(X)\|_{\psi_1}^2\right\|_{\infty} + 2\varepsilon e\max_{k \in [n]}\left\|\|f_k(X)\|_{\psi_1}\right\|_{\infty}} \right).
</math>
}}

===Bennett and Bernstein forms===

Refinements to McDiarmid's inequality in the style of [[Bennett's inequality]] and [[Bernstein inequalities (probability theory)|Bernstein inequalities]] are made possible by defining a variance term for each function argument. Let
: <math>\begin{align}
B &:= \max_{k \in [n]} \sup_{x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_{n}} \left|f(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, X_k, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_n) - \mathbb{E}_{X_k}f(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, X_k, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_n)\right|, \\
V_k &:= \sup_{x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_{n}} \mathbb{E}_{X_k} \left(f(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, X_k, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_n) - \mathbb{E}_{X_k}f(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, X_k, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_n)\right)^2, \\
\tilde \sigma^2 &:= \sum_{k=1}^n V_k.
\end{align}</math>

{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (Bennett form)<ref name="ying" /> |math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> satisfy the bounded differences property with bounds <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math>.
Consider independent random variables <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>. Let <math>B</math> and <math>\tilde\sigma^2</math> be defined as at the beginning of this section.

Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
: <math>
\text{P}(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)] \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{\varepsilon}{2B}\log\left(1+\frac{B\varepsilon}{\tilde\sigma^2}\right)\right).
</math>
}}
{{math theorem |name=McDiarmid's Inequality (Bernstein form)<ref name="ying" /> |math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> satisfy the bounded differences property with bounds <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math>. Let <math>B</math> and <math>\tilde\sigma^2</math> be defined as at the beginning of this section.

Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
: <math>
\text{P}(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)] \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2\left(\tilde\sigma^2 + \frac{B\varepsilon}{3}\right)}\right).</math>
}}

==Proof==

The following proof of McDiarmid's inequality<ref name="Doob" /> constructs the [[Doob martingale]] tracking the [[conditional expected value]] of the function as more and more of its arguments are sampled and conditioned on, and then applies a martingale concentration inequality ([[Azuma's inequality]]).
An alternate argument avoiding the use of martingales also exists, taking advantage of the independence of the function arguments to provide a [[Chernoff bound|Chernoff-bound]]-like argument.<ref name="ying" />

For better readability, we will introduce a notational shorthand: <math>z_{i \rightharpoondown j}</math> will denote <math>z_i, \dots, z_j</math> for any <math>z \in \mathcal{X}^n</math> and integers <math>1 \le i \le j \le n</math>, so that, for example,
: <math>f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, y, x_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) := f(X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1}, y, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n).</math>

Pick any <math>x_1', x_2', \ldots, x_n'</math>. Then, for any <math>x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n</math>, by [[triangle inequality]],
:<math>
\begin{align}
&|f(x_{1 \rightharpoondown n}) - f(x'_{1 \rightharpoondown n})| \\[6pt]
\leq {} & |f(x_{1 \rightharpoondown\, n}) - f(x'_{1 \rightharpoondown (n-1)}, x_n)| + c_n\\
\leq {} & |f(x_{1 \rightharpoondown n}) - f(x'_{1 \rightharpoondown (n-2)}, x_{(n-1) \rightharpoondown n})| + c_{n-1} + c_n\\
\leq {} & \ldots \\
\leq {} & \sum_{i=1}^n c_i ,
\end{align}
</math>
and thus <math>f</math> is bounded.

Since <math>f</math> is bounded, define the Doob martingale <math>\{Z_i\}</math> (each <math>Z_i</math> being a random variable depending on the random values of <math>X_1, \ldots, X_i</math>) as
: <math>Z_i:=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown i} ]</math>
for all <math>i\geq 1</math> and <math>Z_0: = \mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown n})]</math>, so that <math>Z_n = f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown n})</math>.

Now define the random variables for each <math>i</math>
: <math>
\begin{align}
U_i &:= \sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}_i} \mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, x, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_i = x] - \mathbb[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_{i\rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}], \\
L_i &:= \inf_{x \in \mathcal{X}_i} \mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, x, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_i = x] - \mathbb[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_{i\rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}]. \\
\end{align}
</math>
Since <math>X_i, \ldots, X_n</math> are independent of each other, conditioning on <math>X_i = x</math> does not affect the probabilities of the other variables, so these are equal to the expressions
: <math>
\begin{align}
U_i &= \sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}_i} \mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, x, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) - f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_{i\rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}], \\
L_i &= \inf_{x \in \mathcal{X}_i} \mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, x, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) - f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, X_{i\rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}]. \\
\end{align}
</math>

Note that <math>L_i \leq Z_i - Z_{i-1} \leq U_i</math>. In addition,
:<math>
\begin{align}
U_i - L_i &= \sup_{u\in \mathcal{X}_i, \ell \in \mathcal{X}_i}
\mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, u, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}]
-\mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, \ell, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}] \\[6pt]
&=\sup_{u\in \mathcal{X}_i, \ell \in \mathcal{X}_i}
\mathbb{E}[f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, u, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) - f(X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}, l, X_{(i+1) \rightharpoondown n}) \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}] \\
&\leq \sup_{x_u\in \mathcal{X}_i, x_l \in \mathcal{X}_i}
\mathbb{E}[c_i \mid X_{1 \rightharpoondown (i-1)}]  \\[6pt]
&\leq c_i
\end{align}
</math>
Then, applying the [[Azuma's_inequality#A_general_form_of_Azuma's_inequality|general form of Azuma's inequality]] to <math>\left\{Z_i\right\}</math>, we have
:<math>
\text{P}(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) ] \geq \varepsilon )
= \operatorname{P}(Z_n - Z_0 \geq \varepsilon)
\leq \exp \left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}\right).
</math>
The one-sided bound in the other direction is obtained by applying Azuma's inequality to <math>\left\{-Z_i\right\}</math> and the two-sided bound follows from a [[Boole's_inequality|union bound]]. <math>\square</math>
